target: Me pidió que le leyera un cuento antes de dormir.
english: He/she asked me to read a story before bed.
tip: English asks you TO read; Spanish can't. Asking someone else to act takes pedir que + subjunctive: me pidió que le leyera = 'asked that I read'. No infinitive shortcut.

target: El saber escuchar es tan importante como el saber hablar.
english: Knowing how to listen is as important as knowing how to speak.
tip: Where English says 'knowing', Spanish nouns the infinitive: el saber escuchar = 'the to-know-how-to-listen'. Never use an -ndo form as a sentence subject.

target: Me tomó el pelo cuando dijo que había ganado la lotería.
english: He was pulling my leg when he said he had won the lottery.
tip: Spaniards take your hair, not pull your leg: tomar el pelo = tease someone. Me tomó el pelo – he 'took my hair', meaning he was only kidding about the lottery.

target: De haber sabido que iba a llover, me habría llevado el paraguas.
english: Had I known it was going to rain, I would have taken the umbrella.
tip: De + infinitive perfecto – literary/formal alternative to si + pluperfect subjunctive.

target: Ya habrán llegado a esta hora.
english: They must have arrived by now.
tip: Future perfect for past guessing: "Habrá sido difícil" (It must have been hard). Speculation about a past event.

target: Mi novio me regaló flores por nuestro aniversario.
english: My boyfriend gave me flowers for our anniversary.
tip: Gave flowers? Not dio. Spanish has a dedicated verb for gift-giving: regalar. Me regaló flores means gave as a present – dar would sound like a mere handover.

target: Me recordó que tenía que entregar el informe esa semana.
english: She reminded me I had to submit the report that week.
tip: 'Esta semana' becomes 'esa semana' in reported speech (demonstrative shift).

target: ¿Te apetece que pidamos comida a domicilio esta noche? No me apetece cocinar.
english: Do you feel like ordering delivery tonight? I don't feel like cooking.
tip: Apetecer runs backwards like gustar – the plan appeals TO you. ¿Te apetece que pidamos? = does ordering appeal to you? And no me apetece cocinar = cooking doesn't tempt me.

target: Tendrá unos cuarenta años.
english: He's probably about forty years old.
tip: Tendrá doesn't mean he WILL be forty – Spanish uses the future to guess about right now. Tendrá unos cuarenta años = he must be about forty.

target: Pase lo que pase, cuenta conmigo.
english: Whatever happens, count on me.
tip: Pase lo que pase doubles the subjunctive – literally 'let happen what may happen'. That echo pattern is Spanish for 'no matter what'.

target: Mis padres están casados desde hace treinta años.
english: My parents have been married for thirty years.
tip: Thirty years in, and Spanish still uses plain present: están casados desde hace treinta años. Desde hace carries the whole 'have been...for' load, so no perfect tense is needed.

target: El cliente está más satisfecho que el mes pasado.
english: The client is more satisfied than last month.
tip: Comparisons take que – más satisfecho que el mes pasado – even when comparing times. The switch to de comes before numbers (más de cinco); plain comparisons like this one keep que.

target: De haber llegado antes, habríamos encontrado sitio.
english: Had we arrived earlier, we would have found a seat.
tip: No 'si' in sight: de + infinitive packs a whole if-clause. De haber llegado antes = si hubiéramos llegado antes, had we arrived earlier.

target: Se me hinchó la pierna después de la picadura.
english: My leg swelled up after the sting.
tip: Se me hinchó la pierna: the leg swells 'on me'. Spanish frames mishaps as happening TO you – me marks the person affected, and la pierna is the grammatical subject.

target: Mi carro es viejo pero está en buenas condiciones.
english: My car is old but it's in good condition.
tip: Ser for inherent quality (viejo), estar for condition (en buenas condiciones).

target: Huelga decir que su contribución fue fundamental.
english: Needless to say, his contribution was fundamental.
tip: Huelga decir que = needless to say (very formal register).

target: Cabe senalar que estos datos no han sido verificados.
english: It should be noted that this data has not been verified.
tip: Cabe + infinitive = it is fitting/appropriate to (formal register).

target: Ella es médica, pero hoy está de vacaciones.
english: She's a doctor, but today she's on vacation.
tip: Ser for identity (es médica = she's a doctor), estar for current state (está de vacaciones = she's on vacation). Same person, different information → different verb.

target: Ella se da cuenta de todo.
english: She notices everything (lit. she gives herself account of everything).
tip: Tempted by 'realizar'? False friend – it means to carry out, not realize. Spanish 'gives itself account': se da cuenta de todo = she notices everything.

target: Los fines de semana me levanto tarde.
english: On weekends I get up late.
tip: "Los fines de semana" – using "los" with a time expression means "every" or "on." Los lunes = on Mondays. Without "los" it's a specific one.

target: Huelga decir que la puntualidad es fundamental.
english: It goes without saying that punctuality is essential.
tip: Huelga looks like 'strike,' but it's the verb holgar (to be idle): huelga decir = saying it would be idle work – it goes without saying.

target: Tendría unos treinta años cuando empezó la empresa.
english: He must have been about thirty when he started the company.
tip: Tendría here isn't 'would have' – the conditional is Spanish's way of guessing about the past: tendría unos treinta años = he was probably about thirty.

target: Estoy hasta las narices de que no me hagan caso.
english: I'm fed up with being ignored (lit. I'm up to the nostrils).
tip: "Estar hasta las narices" – estar + preposition phrase for emotional state. Similar: "estar harto/a" (to be fed up).

target: Cuanto más estudio, más me doy cuenta de lo que no sé.
english: The more I study, the more I realize what I don't know.
tip: "Cuanto más...más..." = The more...the more: "Cuanto más estudio, más aprendo." Correlative comparative structure.

target: Eso es harina de otro costal; no tiene nada que ver.
english: That's a different kettle of fish (lit. that's flour from another sack) – it has nothing to do with it.
tip: Harina de otro costal, 'flour from another sack': sacks held different grades of flour, so another sack meant a different matter entirely.

target: Se las arregla muy bien sola.
english: She manages very well on her own (lit. she fixes them for herself).
tip: What does 'las' point to in se las arregla? Nothing! Some idioms carry a dummy feminine plural – arreglárselas just means to cope. Stop hunting for the noun.

target: Cuanto más al sur íbamos, más calor hacía.
english: The further south we went, the hotter it got.
tip: English needs 'the' twice in 'the further, the hotter' – Spanish uses none: cuanto más al sur íbamos, más calor hacía. Cuanto opens the pair; bare más answers.

target: No le des más vueltas; ya está decidido.
english: Don't overthink it (lit. don't give it more turns) – it's already decided.
tip: 'Don't give it more turns'? Spanish pictures worrying as spinning a thought: darle vueltas a algo = mull it over. No le des más vueltas = let it go.

target: Es raro que el sistema falle a esta hora.
english: It's strange that the system would fail at this hour.
tip: The system really does fail, yet 'falle' is subjunctive. After es raro que, Spanish marks your reaction to a fact – not the fact itself.

target: Terminada la reunión, todos se dirigieron a la salida.
english: Once the meeting was over, everyone headed for the exit.
tip: 'Terminada la reunión' is an absolute participial clause: participle + noun = 'once X was done'.
